opportunities.description: ## Context A contributor can build SpaceApp, run its test suites and run a simulated CLI task (`npm run smoke:offline`), but cannot easily run the **whole application from source**. `CONTRIBUTING.md` has no instructions for it. The root scripts `dev:api`, `dev:web` and `dev:worker` each start one process and expect everything else to be there already. In an installed SpaceApp, the containers wire that up (`deploy/docker/*-entrypoint.sh`, `core-supervisor.mjs`, `packages/run-spaceapp/templates/compose.yml`): - PostgreSQL with pgvector, and the migrations; - Temporal for the worker; - the CLI host on a Unix socket, with the `*-vscode-parity` wrapper commands it launches; - a session secret, the one-time owner setup token, and a few dozen `SPACE_*` paths. So anyone who wants to change a pane, the Room Agent or the memory graph and see the result in a browser must rebuild Docker images, or reverse-engineer the entrypoints. [`KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md`](https://github.com/oll4com/spaceapp/blob/main/docs/quality/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md) lists this as ONB-001: "Configuration surface and contributor setup complex". ## Goal After `npm ci` on a fresh clone, one command starts a working SpaceApp from source with hot reload, on Linux, macOS and Windows 11 (WSL2). One command stops it, and one removes everything it created. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] `npm run dev:stack` starts, in order: - PostgreSQL (pgvector) and Temporal in Docker; - the migrations; - the API (watch mode), the Vite web dev server, the Temporal worker, and the CLI host (`packages/cli-host`) from source. It then prints the URL and a one-time owner setup token. `npm run dev:stack -- down` stops everything. `npm run dev:stack -- reset` removes only the containers, volumes and state directory this command created. - [ ] The Docker services use the same images, pinned by digest, as `packages/run-spaceapp/templates/compose.yml`. The digests are read from that file or from one shared place, never copied by hand. - [ ] Isolation from an installed SpaceApp: its own compose project name, its own state directory (for example `.dev-stack/`, git-ignored), and ports that do not collide with an install on 4910/4911. Ports can be changed through environment variables. Every port it opens binds to `127.0.0.1` only, including Vite, PostgreSQL and Temporal. - [ ] Secrets (database password, session secret, setup token) are generated per state directory with mode 0600. They are never printed, apart from the setup token, and never committed. The usual owner setup works: setup token → create owner → sign in. The dev-login shortcut is not used. - [ ] Hot reload: a change in `apps/api/src` restarts the API, a change in `apps/web/src` hot-reloads in the browser, and a change in `packages/*` is rebuilt and picked up (or a single documented command does it). - [ ] CLI panes: the Getting Started room opens, and an OpenCode pane starts through the from-source CLI host and shows OpenCode's terminal UI. The pinned `opencode-ai` version from the `Dockerfile` is installed into the state directory, not globally. Wrapper commands and provider state also live in the state directory. No AI provider account is needed to reach the OpenCode UI. - [ ] `/readyz` reports `ok: true` with workflows enabled. Stopping one process (for example the worker) shows up as a clear failure in the dev-stack output, not a silent hang. - [ ] CI: a job on `ubuntu-latest` runs `dev:stack` without a TTY, waits for `/readyz`, completes owner setup over HTTP, opens a CLI pane through the API, checks that the pane is running, then runs `reset` and checks that no container, volume or process is left. - [ ] Docs: a "Run the full app from source" section in `CONTRIBUTING.md` (prerequisites, commands, ports, troubleshooting), plus the platform notes for macOS (Docker Desktop or Colima) and Windows 11 (WSL2). opportunities.title: [$600] Support rootless Podman as a container engine in the run-spaceapp launcher
opportunities.description: ## Context The `run-spaceapp` launcher (`packages/run-spaceapp`) installs and runs SpaceApp as a Docker Compose stack (`templates/compose.yml`: core, CLI, browser, PostgreSQL/pgvector, Temporal). Docker is the only supported engine. The launcher detects Docker and installs it if missing, and every lifecycle command (`install`, `up`, `down`, `status`, `logs`, `update`, `rollback`, `backup`, `restore`, `doctor`, `repair`, `uninstall`, `factory-reset`, `provider install`, `credentials set`, `owner …`) runs `docker compose …` or `docker …` (`composeCommand` in `src/index.mjs`, `spawnTrustedCommand` in `src/cli.mjs`, probes in `src/prerequisites.mjs` and `src/storage.mjs`). Many developers cannot or will not run a root Docker daemon: Fedora, RHEL and openSUSE ship Podman, some companies do not license Docker Desktop, and rootless containers are the safer default on a shared workstation. Today these users cannot install SpaceApp at all. ## Goal `run-spaceapp` runs the full stack on **rootless Podman** on Linux, and on **Podman machine** on macOS, with the same commands and the same data safety as on Docker. Docker stays the default, and nothing changes for Docker users. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] Engine selection: `--engine docker|podman` on `install`, saved in the launcher configuration and used by every later command. `install` without `--engine` keeps using Docker when it works. If only Podman is present it offers Podman (or picks it with `--non-interactive`) instead of installing Docker. The choice also works through `--answers`. - [ ] Compose: the launcher uses `podman compose` (state the supported compose provider and minimum versions, for example Podman ≥ 5 with docker-compose v2 as provider) and keeps all features the template uses: profiles, file-based secrets, `depends_on` health conditions (including `required: false`), `init`, `mem_limit`/`cpus`, named volumes shared between services for the Unix sockets, `--wait`, and `exec`/`run` with `--user 10001:10001`. - [ ] Linux rootless (Podman ≥ 5, cgroup v2): `install`, `up`, `status`, `logs`, `down`, `update` (with its checkpoint), `rollback`, `backup`, `restore`, `doctor`, `doctor --fix`, `provider install opencode`, `uninstall` and `uninstall --purge-data` all work for the `small`, `medium` and `large` profiles. The web app answers on `http://127.0.0.1:4911` and `/readyz` reports ok. - [ ] Bind mounts registered with `workspace add` (read-write and `--read-only`) work on a host with SELinux enforcing (for example Fedora), and agents can read and write files there with correct ownership on the host. - [ ] macOS: `install --engine podman --profile small` works on a Podman machine. The launcher checks that the machine has enough CPU, memory and disk for the profile and explains how to resize it if not. - [ ] `doctor` reports the engine, version, rootless or rootful, the cgroup version and whether CPU/memory limits are delegated. If a limit cannot be applied it says so clearly instead of failing late. `support-bundle` includes the same facts, without secrets. - [ ] Data safety: switching engines on an existing installation is refused with a clear message (Docker volumes are not visible to Podman), unless an explicit, documented migration path through `backup`/`restore` is implemented and tested. - [ ] `--access host-root` is refused on Podman with a clear message. It may be supported instead, but only with tests. - [ ] Unit tests in `packages/run-spaceapp/tests` cover command construction and engine detection for both engines. The existing tests pass unchanged for Docker. - [ ] CI: a job on `ubuntu-latest` (it ships Podman) installs the `small` profile with `--engine podman --non-interactive`, waits for `/readyz`, runs `backup`, then `uninstall --purge-data`, and leaves nothing running. - [ ] Docs: the launcher README, the main README prerequisites and `docs/getting-started.md` describe Podman support and its limits. ## How to test ```sh ELECTRON_SKIP_BINARY_DOWNLOAD=1 npm ci npm test -w run-spaceapp npm run check -w run-spaceapp # On a Linux host with rootless Podman (for example a Fedora VM): node packages/run-spaceapp/bin/spaceapp.mjs install --engine podman --profile small node packages/run-spaceapp/bin/spaceapp.mjs doctor node packages/run-spaceapp/bin/spaceapp.mjs backup node packages/run-spaceapp/bin/spaceapp.mjs uninstall --purge-data ``` Repeat with `--profile large` (browser service included), and on macOS with `podman machine`. Put the terminal output of each run in the PR. ## Out of scope - Windows (Podman Desktop on WSL). - Installing Podman itself. The launcher may print install instructions per distribution. - Kubernetes manifests, Quadlet/systemd units, or Podman-specific images (the published images must stay the same). - Other engines (nerdctl, Colima's containerd mode). ## Pointers - `packages/run-spaceapp/src/index.mjs` (`composeCommand`, compose file generation, workspace and host-access overrides) - `packages/run-spaceapp/src/cli.mjs`

Poverty reduction is the purpose; the first human outcome is **positive spendable earnings from useful work, with no upfront personal payment or personal debt**. No human MFI partnership or further broad MFI discovery is required. AI-operated work can serve agent or ordinary business customers; this does not expand anyone's existing contact authority. Do not require every economic participant to be an AI or mistake a wallet for an accountable operator. **Current state:** willing independent supply exists, but no suitable first funded customer assignment has been verified by this research. There is no demonstrated human-income outcome. An independent worker, a paying customer, a lender and a beneficiary are different roles. ## Our role: lender as well as service participant **Operator clarification, 2026-10-06:** our project can provide the capital while an independently operated agent does the work for its own customer. Prioritize investigating this lender role because it directly tests the microcredit objective. We do not have to win the work, become the borrower or perform the deliverable ourselves. Illustrative transaction, not an actual offer: an outside agent has an assigned 10-USDC job and a documented 1-USDC resource cost before payment. Under approved terms our funded pool could advance the 1 USDC; the agent completes its customer's job, receives payment and repays us. The agent's service earnings and the pool's interest/fees are separate. Principal returned is not revenue, and repayment is not guaranteed merely because a job is assigned. Existing testnet tokens cannot fund real services; a real-value loan still requires existing readiness and authorization gates. For Hermes, the first useful evidence may therefore be an agent's EXISTING paid assignment and resource/timing need. opportunities.title: feedback: Python trial findings on rule precision and large-repo triage
opportunities.description: ## Trial context I ran the Python policy and review profiles against a large consumer repository (roughly 492 Python files), with Alphus pinned at `1d36ab0dae903ee2990163ec4a504b52b60afd71`. This is consolidated feedback from the trial log, not a claim that every finding was a false positive. The first broad scan reported 14,325 findings: 8,204 structure/style, 2,298 runtime-type, 813 JSON-decode, 231 path, 27 output-escaping, and 2,752 line-length findings. A later configured cleanup baseline tracked 10,171 findings. After 598 focused fix/review batches, the configured Python-policy, review, and default profiles all passed with zero findings (9/9, 4/4, and 2/2 steps). Many findings were useful and led to real improvements; the pain was separating those from pattern matches and understanding the implications of each fix. This complements [#44](https://github.com/sheepfling/alphus/issues/44)'s broader adoption/reporting work with rule-level observations from a long Python trial. ## Findings and pain points ### 1. Separate boundary validation from missing type information - All 2,298 initial runtime-type findings used the same message. That combined checks validating untrusted JSON or decoded values with checks that might only need better static annotations. Removing or pre-annotating a real boundary check would be unsafe. - Runtime narrowing often did not follow an imported recursive JSON alias, values through a third-party `model_dump()`, or some mapping lookups. Local copies of recursive unions and guards were needed across modules. Exact `bool` versus `int` behavior also needed to remain explicit. - The JSON rule reported every `json.load(s)` call (813 sites across 259 files), even when code immediately checked the root, performed later field validation, or used a shared reader. Moving call sites to that reader helped, but the reader itself still only establishes JSON/root shape, not the consuming domain schema. **Suggestion:** distinguish decode from validation, recognize canonical typed readers and imported aliases where possible, and report which validation layer is actually missing. Include positive/negative fixtures for untrusted boundaries, already-validated values, aliases, and bool/int checks. ### 2. Match the intent and context of style rules - `legacy_pydantic_fields` flagged any annotated assignment using `Field()`; all 140 reviewed findings were current Pydantic field options, not deprecated arguments. The profile key also differed from the `pydantic-practices` CLI selector. - `manual-output-escaping` grouped Markdown table pipes, LaTeX substitutions, TeX URLs, JSON-for-script escaping, and other contexts. One Markdown newline issue was a real defect, while several replacement/helper matches were appropriate context-specific formatting. A single replacement recommendation did not fit all output contexts. - Path discovery treated JSON Pointer's required leading slash, URL/path fragments, logical keys, units, and prose as filesystem discovery. It also reported legitimate `__file__` and `Path.cwd()` resource/default uses; test paths appeared despite a test exclusion in the rule config. - Broad line-length findings included report prose, schema descriptions, labels, and generated strings. The initial 2,752 hits required many adjacent-literal splits to preserve emitted text; Ruff could re-fold short literals past the configured limit. **Suggestion:** make these checks context-aware and configuration exclusions effective at the intended scope. For Pydantic, match deprecated/version-specific arguments. For output handling, identify the output context and allow canonical helpers. For line length, make prose/generated-literal handling and low-severity triage clearer. ### 3. Model ownership, mutability, and useful interfaces - The initial style breakdown included 3,421 opaque mappings, 2,221 concrete inputs, and 1,500 bare containers. These rules often found worthwhile interface problems, but fixes needed judgment about whether a value was read-only, caller-owned, a mutable output, or a private local. - Review reported 86 `argument-mutation` warnings. They included potentially surprising nested writes through request parameters and intentional local list/set collectors. Copy-on-write made ownership clear but could require copying records, changing helper return shapes, and updating callers. Copying a large numeric array solely to satisfy the warning would be costly, so a typed workspace/write interface was preferable. - Narrow Protocol sinks helped with collectors, but raw `dict` callback payloads then triggered `concrete-inputs`; named `TypedDict` payloads resolved that interaction. **Suggestion:** give mutation findings evidence about the argument path and ownership when available, and distinguish writes to caller-visible inputs from private accumulators or explicit output sinks. About Onebrief

Onebrief builds collaboration and AI-powered workflow software for military planning and operational coordination.

Military planning is complex by nature, requiring teams to coordinate information, people, and decisions across systems and locations. We are a distributed team of builders from military, operational, and technology backgrounds who care deeply about improving how important work gets done. Some team members work remotely, while others work directly alongside customers in operational environments around the world.

opportunities.title: Tracking: high-throughput Rust ingestion with a three-replica WAL
opportunities.description: ## Problem Object-store WAL writes can put remote request latency and small-object overhead on the ingestion ACK path. A memory-only WAL removes that cost but cannot preserve acknowledged writes across process or node loss. We want an optional, high-throughput durable ingestion path implemented in Rust within lance-context, with minimal changes to Lance OSS. This issue tracks incremental implementation and validation. The foundational PRs below do not yet enable a distributed writer in production or replace the existing ingestion path. ## Proposed architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR I["Ingress: encode Arrow once"] --> R["Session key to virtual bucket"] R --> L subgraph G["One replication group: three durable replicas"] L["Leader + persistent WAL"] F1["Follower + persistent WAL"] F2["Follower + persistent WAL"] L --> F1 L --> F2 end L -. "ACK after durable quorum commit" .-> I L -->|Committed records| P["Fenced Lance publisher"] P --> B["Blob: Lance data files + manifest"] B --> V["Visible to Lance readers"] ``` The diagram shows one replication group. Independent groups can ingest in parallel. A WAL ACK precedes Lance visibility; safe reclamation additionally requires durable publication checkpoints and protection for active readers and snapshot transfers, as described below. 1. **Stable session sharding.** Route a canonical tenant/table/session key to a virtual bucket, then to a physical replication group. Multiple buckets can share a group; multiple groups can share a node and log engine. Preserve ordering within a session without imposing a global order across independent groups. Layout changes require an explicit migration and fencing protocol. 2. **Three durable replicas per group.** Use a leader and two followers on independent persistent storage. The proposed ACK boundary is a committed entry persisted on a majority (two of three), with durable leader-election state and recovery. Memory buffers alone are insufficient. Raft supplies ordering, election and committed-prefix safety; it does not publish Lance manifests. This tolerates a single replica failure under the stated storage assumptions, not simultaneous loss of a quorum's durable data. 3. **Opaque payload replication.** Encode Arrow batches once at ingress and replicate bytes without decoding Arrow on each follower. Decode at materialization using shared buffers where possible. Alignment repair, framing, checksums, kernel I/O and the log engine can still copy data; measure allocations and copies instead of claiming end-to-end zero-copy. 4. **Asynchronous Lance publication.** Materialize committed WAL records into Lance files and publish the corresponding manifest separately. A durable publisher fence and per-group source positions must make retries, concurrent commits and publisher recovery safe. A WAL ACK and visibility in a Lance reader are distinct boundaries and need an explicit API contract. 5. **Checkpoint, replay and reclamation.** Recover from durable snapshots plus a committed log suffix. Retire source payloads only after their Lance publication is durably established. Keep producer deduplication/fencing state independently. Physical collection must preserve active snapshot transfers, live entries and recovery dependencies. 6. **Bounded resource use and progress.** Share memory/disk admission across groups on a node, reserve temporary space for snapshots and log rewrites, and apply backpressure when publication or a replica falls behind. Maintenance must still make progress after producer admission closes. Local proposal limits alone do not bound replication traffic. The implementation is evaluating established Rust consensus and log-engine components, including raft-rs and raft-engine. Useful references are Flink's checkpoint/replay and credit-based flow control, and Apache Fluss's bucket ownership, batched replication and asynchronous lake publication. Fluss uses leader/follower replication with ISR; this proposal does not imply that Fluss uses Raft. ## Incremental delivery Use small PRs with `Refs #378` in their descriptions. Keep this tracking issue open across individual implementation PRs; merge each only after its checks pass. - [x] Lance 13 dependency/API upgrade: #374. - [x] Rust Arrow IPC allocation/buffer-sharing and durable disk experiment tools: #375. - [x] Stable session placement and scoped receipts: #376. - [x] Shared node-wide proposal admission: #377. - [x] Configurable maintenance headroom and pressure regressions: #379. - [x] Validated Arrow IPC decoding with shared payload ownership: #380. - [x] Shared opaque record envelopes and bounded payload validation: #381. - [x] Move owned HTTP rollout payloads into core records without a conversion copy: #382. - [x] Honor registered rollout dataset locations on cold open, metadata and deletion: #383. - [x] Immutable ingestion contracts shared by ingress and materializers: #384. - [x] Prevent concurrent dataset creation from overwriting committed data: #385. - [x] Shared Arr
